name: Cenchrus
common_group: sandburs and bristlegrasses (including buffelgrass in modern broad Cenchrus)

project_scope.selection_mode: recognition-first genus lesson; species installer independent
project_scope.native_target_zone_status: NOT_ASSESSED — BONAP/NAPA county verification required per species
project_scope.caution: Some native sandburs and introduced or invasive grasses belong to Cenchrus. Genus recognition does not confer native-range PASS.

look_here_first: On a flowering or fruiting grass, find a dense, spike-like axis bearing separate BURRS or BRISTLY CLUSTERS. Turn one cluster sideways: the bristles surround one or more small grass SPIKELETS rather than being petals or an individual grass seed. A young grass without heads should remain unidentified to genus unless supporting features are documented.

genus_diagnostics.habit: Annual and perennial grasses; tufted, erect, ascending or sprawling forms. Size and growth form differ substantially among taxa.
genus_diagnostics.leaf: Typical grass node, sheath, blade and collar. Inspect the LIGULE as a hair fringe when visible, but this alone does not diagnose Cenchrus.
genus_diagnostics.inflorescence: Panicle commonly contracted into a dense spike-like array, sometimes with bristly units surrounding spikelets. Bur-bearing species have stiff, sometimes barbed or fused basal bristles that detach as a unit.
genus_diagnostics.spikelet: Each apparent bur or bristly fascicle may contain one or multiple grass spikelets. Separate bristles (modified branch structures) from GLUMES, LEMMAS, and PALEAS.
genus_diagnostics.fruit: Grass caryopsis enclosed in associated spikelet parts; dispersal structures vary by species. Do not treat the whole detachable bur as one naked seed.
genus_diagnostics.taxonomy: Modern broad Cenchrus includes taxa historically placed in Pennisetum. Many non-spiny bottlebrush grasses share the genus, so a painful bur cannot define the entire genus.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: whole inflorescence → individual detached bur/bristle fascicle → enclosed spikelets → ligule/collar → taxon-level comparison

steps.title: 1 · See the whole head
steps.look_for: Multiple discrete bur clusters attached along a common central axis, not one solid seed head.

steps.title: 2 · Open one bur
steps.photo_role: macro of bur with surrounding bristles and enclosed spikelets
steps.look_for: The outer prickles/bristles are NOT seed coats. Look within for the real spikelets.

steps.title: 3 · Show the grass collar
steps.photo_role: leaf sheath, ligule hair fringe and blade
steps.look_for: Find the hairy ligule at the junction of sheath and blade; compare against look-alike grasses.

steps.title: 4 · Compare spiny and non-spiny Cenchrus
steps.photo_role: native-region sandbur versus introduced buffelgrass/Pennisetum-type bristle head
steps.look_for: Bristles may be fused and rigid in sandburs, or slender and soft in other members of broad Cenchrus.

comparison_cards.title: Cenchrus spinifex vs Cenchrus longispinus
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Compare several mature BURRS and exposed spikelets under a ruler or macro rather than guessing from one spine.
comparison_cards.field_note: Both are accepted North American sandbur species with overlapping general appearance. Species-level distinction requires a formal regional key and measured mature bur characters.

comparison_cards.title: Sandburs vs Setaria (foxtails)
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Both can have bristles, but sandbur-type Cenchrus has distinct spiny or fused bur units enclosing spikelets; Setaria typically shows a spike-like foxtail with separate bristles subtending individual spikelets.
comparison_cards.caution: Modern broader Cenchrus includes nonspiny bristlegrasses; use reproductive architecture and taxonomy, not prickliness alone.

comparison_cards.title: Cenchrus vs other spiky grass seed heads
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Separate the central rachis, enclosing bristles/bur, and actual spikelets. Do not call individual spines awns without checking their point of attachment.

safety_and_field_notes: Use forceps and gloves when opening barbed burrs; do not press into skin.
Disturbed ground or a city trail is a habitat clue, never proof of a species or native provenance.
Do not install genus-level images as exact species until taxon ID, rights and photo roles are verified.

photo_requirements.role: in situ paired burs and ruler
